motion: Did Jesus rise from the dead, and does the surviving historical evidence justify preferring resurrection to natural or legendary alternatives?

burdenRoutes.description: A historical-inference route from early appearance testimony and bodily-resurrection content through comparative explanatory performance to preference for resurrection.
burdenRoutes.successCriteria: The surviving evidence must establish the relevant resurrection reports and make bodily resurrection a better historical explanation than the identified natural or legendary alternatives.

bridges.description: The compared surviving evidence warrants preferring Jesus's bodily resurrection over the identified natural or legendary alternatives, affirming the motion.
Early testimony establishes that relevant witnesses sincerely reported individual and group appearances interpreted as the risen Jesus.
On the stated historical criteria, resurrection explains the locked appearance evidence better than the identified natural or legendary alternatives.
Paul's received-and-delivered formulation is early and connected enough to the Jerusalem witnesses to carry historical evidential weight.
The reported individual, group, friend, and foe appearances resist the proposed hallucination mechanisms.
The earliest resurrection claim concerns Jesus's transformed physical corpse rather than only a disembodied vision.
Jesus's prior claims, predicted resurrection, and reportedly significant deeds make the later appearance reports evidentially distinctive.

burdenRoutes.description: A comparative route from the low observed frequency of resurrection and ordinary causal mechanisms to the conclusion that the evidence does not justify resurrection preference.
burdenRoutes.successCriteria: Ordinary natural or legendary alternatives must remain at least as well supported by the surviving evidence, leaving the resurrection preference unjustified.

bridges.description: Natural or legendary alternatives remain at least as well supported, so the evidence does not justify preferring resurrection and the motion is defeated.
The very low observed frequency of resurrection imposes an exceptional evidential threshold that the surviving record does not meet.
Known natural or legendary processes explain the relevant reports without requiring an actual resurrection.
Ordinary displacement, theft, or misidentification remains a live explanation for any missing-body report.
Individual or socially guided hallucination remains a live explanation for the reported appearances.
Ancient charismatic religious settings can gather vision-prone participants and shape mutually reinforcing experiences.
Paul's outsider conversion can arise from rare but ordinary psychological mechanisms rather than a real appearance.
The epistles and later narratives do not supply sufficiently detailed, independent evidence to exclude ordinary explanations.
The limited distribution of reported appearances better fits a local religious movement than a universally compassionate divine intervention.

source.limitations: Human English captions have no diarization and contain recognition artifacts. Speaker ownership was accepted only inside explicit moderated turns or uninterrupted closing statements; rapid mixed-turn caption events were excluded without audio verification.
